title: The two-chair swap: argue the other side
description: Pick a friendly disagreement, set two chairs facing each other, and take turns arguing the OTHER person's position for two minutes. You cannot rebut — only represent.

body.heading: How the swap runs
paragraphs: Choose a low-stakes disagreement — where to holiday, whether the cat should be allowed in the bedroom. Person A states their own view in one minute. Then A sits in the other chair and argues B's view for two minutes, as fairly as they can, while B listens without correcting.
Then swap roles. The round ends with each person saying what surprised them about holding the other position — not who won.

body.heading: Why representing beats rebutting
paragraphs: Arguing a view you oppose forces you to find its strongest form, which is the fastest way to discover what the disagreement is actually about. Often it shrinks: the two positions turn out to share a value and differ only on method.

Groups that practise the swap argue better everywhere else, because listening-to-represent becomes a habit, not a technique. Keep it playful and time-boxed, and retire any topic that stops being friendly.

takeaway: Argue the other person's position for two minutes from their chair — representing a view fairly is the quickest way to understand it.
materials: A low-stakes disagreement chosen in advance
supervision: One person keeps time and enforces the no-rebuttal rule; anyone may retire a topic that stops feeling friendly.
safetyNotes: Choose light topics only — never use the swap for grievances, money disputes or anything involving a third person's feelings.
Either person may stop the exercise at any time, no reason needed.
